parts.label: Concepts
parts.body:
## Why this lesson exists

The intro RAG lesson gave you the pipeline: parse, chunk, embed, index, retrieve, generate. This lesson zooms into the two decisions that quietly cap the quality of everything downstream: **how you cut documents into chunks** and **how you turn those chunks into vectors**. A reranker or a stronger LLM cannot recover a passage that was never retrieved, and a passage cannot be retrieved if the chunk boundaries split the answer in half or the vector for it says "this is about the table of contents".

A useful mental model: retrieval is a **lossy compression** problem. You compress each chunk of text into a single point in a few hundred to a few thousand dimensions, then hope that the question's point lands near the right chunk's point. Every choice in this lesson changes what information survives the compression.

## What an embedding actually is

A text embedding model is (almost always today) a transformer encoder, or a decoder LLM adapted to act like one, that reads a sequence of tokens and produces one vector per token. To get **one vector per text** it **pools** those token vectors:

| Pooling | How | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| CLS pooling | Take the vector of a special first token | Original BERT-style models |
| Mean pooling | Average all token vectors (ignoring padding) | Sentence-BERT family, many open models |
| Last-token pooling | Take the final token's vector | Decoder-based embedding models |

The model is then trained **contrastively**: pairs that should match (question and its answer passage, title and abstract, duplicate questions) are pulled together, and every other passage in the batch is pushed away (the in-batch negatives trick). Harder negatives (passages that look relevant but are not) make the model sharper. This training objective is the reason embeddings capture "aboutness" and paraphrase, and also the reason they are weak at things the training pairs rarely tested: exact identifiers, negation ("not refundable" vs "refundable"), numbers and rare names.

### Asymmetric retrieval and instructions

A question ("how long do EU refunds take?") and its answer passage ("Refunds for customers in the EU are processed within 14 days...") look nothing alike as text. Models trained for **asymmetric** retrieval handle this by treating queries and documents differently:

- Some expect a text prefix such as `query: ` and `passage: ` (the E5 family) or a task instruction for the query.
- Some API models take an explicit input type (`search_query` / `search_document`, or `query` / `document`).
- OpenAI's `text-embedding-3` models take no input type; the same call embeds both sides.

Forgetting the prefix or input type is one of the most common silent bugs: everything "works", recall is just 5 to 15 points lower than it should be. Read the model card, and put the prefix logic in one function used by both ingestion and query code.

## Dimensions, normalisation and similarity

### Dimensions

Typical output sizes are 384, 768, 1,024, 1,536 and 3,072. More dimensions can hold more nuance but cost linearly in storage, memory and distance computation. The raw arithmetic:

```text
1,000,000 chunks x 1,536 dims x 4 bytes (float32) = 6.1 GB of raw vectors
1,000,000 chunks x   768 dims x 4 bytes           = 3.1 GB
1,000,000 chunks x 1,536 dims x 1 byte  (int8)    = 1.5 GB
1,000,000 chunks x 1,536 dims x 1 bit   (binary)  = 0.19 GB
```

HNSW adds graph links on top of that (with M = 16, roughly 32 neighbour ids per node at layer 0, so another 100 to 200 bytes per vector).

### Matryoshka embeddings

Matryoshka Representation Learning (Kusupati et al., 2022) trains a model so that the **first k dimensions are themselves a good embedding** for several values of k. You can then truncate a 3,072-dim vector to 256 or 1,024 dims and re-normalise, trading a little quality for a large cut in storage and latency. OpenAI's `text-embedding-3-small` (1,536 dims) and `text-embedding-3-large` (3,072 dims) expose this through a `dimensions` parameter, and many open models (Nomic, recent BGE and Jina models, others) are trained the same way. A common production pattern is **shortlist with short vectors, rescore with full vectors**.

### Normalisation and the choice of metric

Three similarity functions dominate:

| Metric | Formula | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Cosine similarity | a.b / (\|a\| \|b\|) | Ignores length, compares direction |
| Dot product | a.b | Equal to cosine when both vectors have length 1 |
| Euclidean (L2) distance | \|a - b\| | For unit vectors, \|a - b\|^2 = 2 - 2 cos(a, b), so the ranking is identical |

So: **if you L2-normalise every vector at write time and every query at read time, cosine, dot product and L2 all produce the same ranking**, and you can use the fastest one (dot product, which is what most ANN libraries optimise). OpenAI's embeddings are returned already normalised to length 1; many open models are not, unless you ask the library to normalise. Mixing normalised documents and unnormalised queries is a classic bug that silently reorders results.

Two more facts worth having ready:

- Absolute similarity values are **not comparable across models** and are often compressed into a narrow band (for some models almost every pair scores between 0.7 and 0.9). Never hard-code a "relevance threshold" like 0.8 without calibrating it on labelled pairs for that exact model.
- **Anisotropy**: embeddings from many models occupy a narrow cone of the space, which is why raw cosine values look uniformly high. Ranking still works; thresholds do not transfer.

## Chunking strategies, in depth

Chunking decides the **unit of retrieval**. The intro lesson listed the strategies; here is how to reason about them.

### The core tension

```text
small chunks (100-200 tokens)          large chunks (800-1500 tokens)
+ one topic per vector, sharp match    + enough context to answer
+ precise citations                    + fewer boundary splits
- answer split across chunks           - vector averages several topics
- pronouns lose their referents        - wastes prompt tokens
- more vectors to store                - "lost in the middle" inside the chunk
```

Embedding a long chunk averages its topics into one point. If a 1,200-token section covers pricing, refunds and shipping, a refund question has to compete with the other two topics for the vector's direction. That is why "bigger chunks = more context = better" is wrong for retrieval, even though it is often right for generation. The fix that resolves the tension is to **decouple the unit you embed from the unit you return** (parent-child, below).

### Strategy by strategy

1. **Fixed-size with overlap.** Split every N tokens with 10 to 20% overlap. Overlap exists so a sentence on the boundary appears whole in at least one chunk. It is cheap and predictable, and the right baseline to beat. Count tokens with the embedding model's tokenizer, not characters, or you will overflow the model's input limit (OpenAI's embedding models accept 8,191 tokens; many open models cap at 512, and silently truncate beyond it).
2. **Recursive / structural.** Split on the strongest boundary first (headings), then paragraphs, then sentences, until each piece fits. This is LangChain's `RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter` idea and the best default for docs, wikis and markdown. Keep the **heading path** for every chunk.
3. **Semantic chunking.** Embed each sentence, compute the similarity between neighbours, and cut where similarity drops below a percentile. It helps on long unstructured prose (transcripts, essays) and is expensive at ingestion (one embedding per sentence). Published comparisons show mixed results against good structural splitting, so measure before adopting it.
4. **Format-aware chunking.** Code split by function or class using a parser (tree-sitter); tables kept whole with their header row repeated in every chunk; one FAQ item, one product, one ticket per chunk.
5. **Parent-child (small-to-big).** Embed small child chunks (sentences or 100 to 200 tokens) for precise matching, store a pointer to the parent section, and send the parent (or a window around the child) to the LLM. A variant, **sentence-window retrieval**, returns k sentences on each side of the matched one.
6. **Propositions.** Use an LLM to rewrite a passage into atomic, self-contained factual statements ("The EU refund window is 14 days.") and embed those. High precision for fact lookup, expensive to build, and you lose the original phrasing unless you keep the link back to the source.

### The pronoun problem

Chunks lose context. "It is processed within 14 days" is meaningless without knowing "it" is an EU refund. Three escalating fixes:

- **Prepend metadata**: document title plus heading path, embedded with the chunk (`Billing > Refunds > EU customers`). Nearly free and usually worth several points of recall.
- **Contextual retrieval** (next part): an LLM writes a one or two sentence context per chunk.
- **Late chunking** (next part): embed the whole document first, then pool per chunk, so each chunk vector has already "seen" the context.

## How to choose, practically

1. Build a retrieval eval first: 50 to 200 real questions, each labelled with the chunk or document that answers it.
2. Start with structural chunking at about 400 to 600 tokens with heading paths, and the embedding model you can afford.
3. Measure recall@5 and recall@20. Then change **one** variable at a time: chunk size, overlap, contextual headers, embedding model, dimensions.
4. Re-chunking means re-embedding everything, so store the raw parsed text and the chunker version, and make the ingestion job idempotent and resumable.

That eval-driven loop is the real answer to every "what chunk size should I use?" question.

parts.label: Context and models
parts.body:
## Putting context back into chunks

Every chunking strategy fights the same enemy: a chunk on its own does not carry the context needed to retrieve it. Two techniques from 2024 attack this directly, from opposite ends.

### Contextual retrieval (Anthropic)

Anthropic's "Contextual Retrieval" write-up proposes a simple ingestion step: for every chunk, ask a small, cheap LLM to write a short (roughly 50 to 100 token) piece of context that situates the chunk within its whole document, then **prepend that context to the chunk before both embedding and BM25 indexing**.

```text
original chunk:
  "The company's revenue grew by 3% over the previous quarter."

contextualised chunk:
  "This chunk is from ACME Corp's Q2 2023 SEC filing; the previous quarter's
   revenue was $314M. The company's revenue grew by 3% over the previous quarter."
```

The prompt is essentially: here is the whole document, here is one chunk, give a short context to situate this chunk for search retrieval, answer with the context only. The full document goes in the prompt for every chunk, which would be expensive, except that it is the **same prefix** for all chunks of a document, so **prompt caching** makes the repeated document tokens cheap. Anthropic estimated a one-time cost of about $1.02 per million document tokens with caching at the time of writing.

Their reported results on their own benchmark mix (codebases, fiction, papers): measured as the failure rate of retrieving the relevant chunk in the top 20, contextual embeddings cut failures by 35%, contextual embeddings plus contextual BM25 by 49%, and adding a reranker on top by 67%. Treat the exact numbers as their datasets; the direction (context plus hybrid plus rerank compounds) has been reproduced widely.

Trade-offs to state in an interview:

- Ingestion cost and time grow with the number of chunks (one LLM call each). Fine for a few million chunks; think hard at billions.
- A document that changes requires regenerating context for its chunks. Hash the document, not just the chunk.
- The generated context can be wrong. Keep the original chunk text separate so the generator quotes the source, not the summary.
- It needs the whole document in the context window. Very long documents need a section-level summary instead.

### Late chunking (Jina)

Late chunking (Günther et al., 2024) flips the order of operations. Normal ("early") chunking splits first and embeds each chunk independently, so the transformer never sees the surrounding text. Late chunking:

1. Runs the **whole document** (up to the model's long context, for example 8,192 tokens) through the embedding transformer once, producing one contextualised vector per token.
2. Splits the **token vectors** at chunk boundaries afterwards.
3. Mean-pools each span into a chunk embedding.

Because attention already mixed information across the document, the token vectors for "it is processed within 14 days" already encode that "it" refers to the EU refund mentioned two paragraphs earlier. No extra LLM calls, no extra text.

Constraints that matter in practice:

- It needs access to **token-level outputs** of a long-context, mean-pooling model. Most hosted embedding APIs only return the pooled vector, so you cannot do it with them (some providers, Jina included, expose a late-chunking option).
- Documents longer than the model's window need a sliding window with overlap ("long late chunking").
- Gains are largest for short chunks with heavy cross-references, and smaller when chunks are already self-contained.

### Comparison

| Approach | Extra ingestion cost | Works with any embedding API | Helps BM25 too | Best when |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Heading path prefix | None | Yes | Yes | Always (do this first) |
| Contextual retrieval | 1 small LLM call per chunk (cached document prefix) | Yes | Yes | Documents with implicit references, financial and legal text |
| Late chunking | One long forward pass per document | No, needs token outputs | No | Self-hosted long-context embedder, many short chunks |
| Parent-child | More vectors, a parent store | Yes | Yes | Precise matching but answers need surrounding context |

## Choosing an embedding model

### What to look at

| Factor | What to check |
|---|---|
| Retrieval quality | MTEB (Muennighoff et al., 2022) retrieval scores to shortlist; your own eval decides |
| Domain and language | Code, legal, biomedical and non-English queries often reorder the leaderboard |
| Max tokens | Chunks beyond it are silently truncated |
| Dimensions and Matryoshka support | Storage, memory and latency at your scale |
| Query/document asymmetry | Required prefixes or input types |
| Hosting | API (no ops, data leaves your network, per-token price) vs self-hosted (GPU, latency control, data stays) |
| Stability | Will the provider deprecate the model? Re-embedding 50M chunks is a project |

The MTEB leaderboard is a shortlist, not an answer. Its retrieval average spans many unrelated datasets, some models have been tuned on data close to the benchmark's, and your users' questions look nothing like BEIR's. A 2-point leaderboard gap routinely flips on a domain eval.

### Quantising vectors

Storage and memory, not compute, usually become the bottleneck first. Options, in order of aggressiveness:

1. **Fewer dimensions** (Matryoshka truncation, then re-normalise).
2. **float16 / bfloat16**: half the bytes, essentially free in quality.
3. **Scalar int8**: map each dimension's range to 256 levels, 4x smaller than float32. Small recall loss, usually recovered by rescoring.
4. **Binary**: one bit per dimension (sign), 32x smaller, compared with Hamming distance, which is extremely fast. Larger quality loss, so it is used as a first-stage shortlist (for example top 200) followed by **rescoring with the full-precision vectors** stored on disk.
5. **Product quantisation (PQ)**: covered in the next lesson.

### Migrating models

Vectors from different models live in different spaces; you cannot compare them. A model migration is a dual-write project:

```text
1. add column/collection embedding_v2 with model name + version
2. backfill v2 for all chunks (batch API, rate-limited, resumable)
3. dual-write new and changed chunks to v1 and v2
4. run the retrieval eval on v2; shadow-query v2 in production and compare
5. switch reads to v2, keep v1 for rollback, then delete it
```

Store `embedding_model`, `embedding_dims`, `chunker_version` and a `content_hash` with every vector. Without them you cannot do incremental re-indexing or safe migrations.

## Ingestion engineering details that bite

- **Batching**: embedding APIs accept many inputs per request (OpenAI allows up to 2,048 inputs per request, subject to a per-request token limit). Batch to cut overhead, and respect rate limits with a token bucket and retry with backoff on 429.
- **Batch APIs**: for large backfills, the asynchronous batch endpoints (OpenAI Batch, 24-hour window) are priced at roughly half the synchronous rate.
- **Idempotency**: key every chunk by `doc_id + chunk_index + content_hash`. Re-running ingestion should be a no-op for unchanged content.
- **Deletes**: when a document is deleted or a section removed, delete its chunks. Orphaned chunks are a common source of "the bot quotes a policy we removed last year".
- **Permissions**: copy ACLs to every chunk at ingestion and re-sync them when permissions change, which is often more frequent than content changes.
- **Empty and duplicate chunks**: boilerplate (footers, cookie banners, "Table of contents") produces many near-identical vectors that crowd out real results. Deduplicate by hash and by near-duplicate detection (MinHash or high cosine similarity) before indexing.

code.source:
# Late chunking: encode the whole document once, then mean-pool token vectors per chunk span.
# Needs a long-context, mean-pooling embedding model whose token outputs you can access (self-hosted).
import numpy as np
import torch
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer

MODEL = "jinaai/jina-embeddings-v2-small-en"   # 8k-token context, mean pooling
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL)
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(MODEL, trust_remote_code=True).eval()


def late_chunk(doc: str, spans: list[tuple[int, int]]) -> np.ndarray:
    """spans are (start_char, end_char) chunk boundaries from any chunker."""
    batch = tok(doc, return_tensors="pt", return_offsets_mapping=True, truncation=True, max_length=8192)
    offsets = batch.pop("offset_mapping")[0].tolist()
    with torch.no_grad():
        tokens = model(**batch).last_hidden_state[0]          # [T, d], every token has seen the whole doc
    vecs = []
    for start, stop in spans:
        idx = [i for i, (a, b) in enumerate(offsets) if b > a and a >= start and b <= stop]
        if not idx:                                         # span fell past the truncation point
            vecs.append(np.zeros(tokens.shape[1], dtype=np.float32))
            continue
        v = tokens[idx].mean(dim=0).numpy()
        vecs.append(v / np.linalg.norm(v))
    return np.stack(vecs)

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are testing

Chunking and embedding questions separate people who have shipped RAG from people who have read about it. The interviewer wants to hear that you treat chunking as a **measured** decision, that you understand what an embedding can and cannot represent, that you know the arithmetic of vector storage, and that you have hit the operational problems: silent truncation, mismatched prefixes, unnormalised vectors, model migrations and stale chunks.

## Questions with model answers

### 1. Walk me through how you would chunk a 300-page product manual with tables and code samples.

**Model answer.** I would parse it with a layout-aware parser that preserves headings, tables and code blocks, then chunk structurally: split on headings first, then paragraphs, then sentences, targeting about 400 to 500 tokens measured with the embedding model's tokenizer. Tables stay whole with their header row repeated if I must split them by rows; code blocks are never split mid-block. Every chunk gets its heading path (`Manual > Installation > Network ports`) prepended for embedding and BM25. If the manual cross-references a lot ("as configured above"), I would test contextual retrieval: a small model writes a one-sentence context per chunk with the whole chapter as a cached prompt prefix. I would compare these variants on recall@5 and recall@20 against a labelled set of real support questions before picking one.

### 2. Cosine similarity, dot product or Euclidean distance: which should I use?

**Model answer.** If the vectors are L2-normalised, all three give the same ranking: dot product equals cosine, and squared Euclidean distance is 2 minus 2 times cosine. So I normalise everything at write and query time and use dot product because ANN libraries optimise it. The only real requirement is consistency: use the metric the model was trained with, and never mix normalised documents with unnormalised queries. I also would not hard-code a similarity threshold; raw scores differ across models and are often compressed into a narrow band, so thresholds need calibration on labelled pairs.

### 3. How much memory do 20 million chunks need, and how would you reduce it?

**Model answer.** At 1,536 float32 dimensions, 20M x 1,536 x 4 bytes is about 123 GB of raw vectors, plus HNSW links (on the order of 100 to 200 bytes per vector at M = 16, so another 2 to 4 GB). To cut it: truncate to 512 or 768 dimensions if the model is Matryoshka-trained (a 2 to 3x saving with a small quality loss I would measure), store float16 (another 2x), or use int8 scalar quantisation (4x versus float32) or binary quantisation (32x) as a first stage with full-precision rescoring of the shortlist from disk. PQ in an IVF index is the option for hundreds of millions. Each step gets checked against recall@k on the eval set.

### 4. What is contextual retrieval and when is it worth the cost?

**Model answer.** It is an ingestion step where an LLM writes a short context for each chunk using the full document, and that context is prepended before embedding and BM25 indexing. It fixes chunks that are ambiguous on their own, like "revenue grew 3%" without the company or quarter. The cost is one small-model call per chunk, made affordable by prompt caching because the document prefix repeats. Anthropic reported it cut top-20 retrieval failures by about a third with embeddings alone and around two thirds when combined with BM25 and reranking on their benchmarks. It is worth it when chunks rely on implicit context (filings, contracts, long reports), and less useful for self-contained content like FAQs or product records.

### 5. Explain late chunking. Why can't you do it with every embedding API?

**Model answer.** Normal chunking embeds each chunk in isolation. Late chunking runs the entire document through a long-context embedding model once, gets contextualised token vectors, and only then pools those token vectors over each chunk's span. Each chunk vector has effectively seen the document, so references like "it" or "this plan" resolve. It needs the token-level outputs and a mean-pooling model with a long context window, and most hosted APIs only return one pooled vector per input, so you need a self-hosted model or a provider that exposes the option.

### 6. We want to switch embedding models. What is the plan?

**Model answer.** Vectors from different models are not comparable, so it is a migration. I would add a new vector field tagged with model and version, backfill it with the batch API (resumable, rate-limited), dual-write new and changed chunks, evaluate the new index offline on the retrieval eval and online via shadow queries, then switch reads behind a flag and keep the old vectors for rollback until the new ones are proven. Metadata like `embedding_model`, `dims` and `chunker_version` on every row makes this possible; without it you have to re-embed blind.

### 7. Recall is fine in tests but users still get irrelevant chunks for part numbers like "XR-2041-B". Why?

**Model answer.** Embedding models are trained on semantic pairs and are weak at exact identifiers: tokenisation splits the code into fragments, and the vector captures "some product code" rather than this specific one. The fix is hybrid retrieval: a BM25 or keyword index (with a tokenizer that keeps identifiers intact) fused with the dense results, plus metadata filters when the identifier maps to a field. I would add identifier queries to the eval set as their own slice so this does not regress.

### 8. What signals tell you chunks are too big or too small?

**Model answer.** Too small: the retrieved chunk is relevant but the answer needs the next paragraph, answers cite three adjacent chunks, and the model complains about missing context. Too big: the right document ranks lower than shorter, more focused ones, the prompt is full of irrelevant text, and faithfulness drops because the answer is buried. Both show up in failure analysis of traces: check whether the gold passage was retrieved, at what rank, and whether the retrieved chunk alone contained the answer. Parent-child retrieval resolves the conflict by matching small and returning big.

## Common mistakes

- Choosing chunk size by intuition or a blog post instead of a retrieval eval.
- Counting characters instead of tokens and silently exceeding the embedding model's input limit (truncation drops the end of the chunk with no error).
- Forgetting query or document prefixes or input types for models that require them.
- Mixing normalised and unnormalised vectors, or comparing scores from two different models.
- Hard-coding a similarity threshold copied from another model.
- Splitting tables and code blocks, or dropping heading context.
- Not storing the model name, chunker version and content hash, which makes incremental updates and migrations painful.
- Leaving chunks of deleted documents in the index.

## Numbers to have ready

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| float32 vector, 1,536 dims | about 6 KB |
| 1M x 1,536 float32 | about 6.1 GB |
| int8 / binary compression vs float32 | 4x / 32x |
| Typical chunk size starting point | 300 to 600 tokens, 10 to 20% overlap |
| OpenAI text-embedding-3 small / large dims | 1,536 / 3,072 (truncatable) |
| Common open-model input limit | 512 tokens (long-context models: 8k) |

Normalise all vectors and cosine, dot product and L2 rank identically; never compare scores across models or hard-code thresholds.
Decouple what you embed from what you return: small, context-prefixed chunks for matching, parent sections for generation.

check.q: Documents are embedded and L2-normalised, but query vectors are not normalised. The index uses dot product. What happens?
options: Nothing changes, because dot product is scale-invariant
The ranking for a single query is unchanged, but scores are not comparable across queries
Search fails with a dimension mismatch error
Long queries are always ranked above short ones
check.why: Scaling the query multiplies every document's score by the same factor, so one query's ranking is preserved, but absolute scores and thresholds become meaningless across queries. Unnormalised documents would change rankings.

check.q: What is the key requirement that prevents late chunking from working with most hosted embedding APIs?
options: It needs a GPU with at least 80 GB of memory
It requires an LLM call per chunk
It needs token-level output vectors from a long-context model, while APIs return one pooled vector per input
It only works with binary-quantised vectors
check.why: Late chunking pools contextualised token vectors per span after encoding the whole document; APIs that only expose a pooled embedding cannot provide those token vectors.

check.q: A team uses 1,200-token chunks because 'more context is better', and recall@5 is poor for specific questions. What is the best first fix?
options: Switch to a model with more embedding dimensions
Raise top-k from 5 to 50 and send everything to the LLM
Embed smaller context-prefixed child chunks and return their parent sections to the LLM
Lower the temperature of the generator
check.why: Large chunks average several topics into one vector, which blurs matching. Parent-child keeps sharp vectors for matching while still giving the generator enough context.

parts.label: ANN indexes
parts.body:
## The retrieval funnel

Production retrieval is a funnel of increasingly expensive, increasingly accurate stages:

```text
millions of chunks
   |  stage 1: candidate generation  (ANN vector search + BM25, ~5-30 ms)
   v
~50-200 candidates
   |  stage 2: fusion                 (RRF, ~0 ms)
   v
~50 candidates
   |  stage 3: reranking              (cross-encoder, ~50-300 ms)
   v
~3-10 passages -> the LLM prompt
```

Each stage only has to be good at its own job. Stage 1 must have **high recall** and be cheap per document, because it touches everything. Stage 3 must have **high precision** and can be expensive per document, because it only sees a handful. This lesson goes inside each stage. The intro lesson told you to "use HNSW, hybrid search and a reranker"; here you will learn why those work, which knobs matter and how they fail.

## Why exact search stops scaling

Exact (flat) k-nearest-neighbour search computes the distance from the query to every vector: `O(N d)` per query. At 1M vectors of 768 dims that is about 768M multiply-adds, a few milliseconds of well-vectorised CPU or GPU work. At 100M it is hundreds of milliseconds per query and the vectors no longer fit comfortably in RAM. **Approximate nearest neighbour (ANN)** indexes give up a small amount of recall (the fraction of the true top-k they return) for orders-of-magnitude speed-ups.

The three families you must be able to explain are **graph-based (HNSW)**, **clustering-based (IVF)** and **compression-based (PQ)**, plus how they combine.

## HNSW, properly

Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs (Malkov and Yashunin, 2016) build a multi-layer proximity graph.

### Construction

1. Each new vector gets a random maximum layer, drawn from an exponentially decaying distribution: most nodes live only on layer 0, few reach the top layers. This is a skip list in graph form.
2. Starting from the global entry point at the top layer, greedily walk towards the new vector, layer by layer, down to the node's own top layer.
3. On each layer from there down, run a beam search with width `ef_construction` to find candidate neighbours, and connect the node to up to `M` of them (`2M` on layer 0 in the reference implementation). A heuristic prefers neighbours that are not already close to each other, which keeps long-range links and prevents the graph from fragmenting into clusters.

### Search

Enter at the top layer, greedily move to whichever neighbour is closest to the query until no neighbour improves, drop a layer, repeat. On layer 0, run a beam search keeping the best `ef_search` candidates, then return the top k. The upper layers act like express highways; layer 0 does the precise local search.

### Knobs and costs

| Knob | Effect | Typical |
|---|---|---|
| `M` | Links per node: recall and memory go up together | 12 to 48 (pgvector default 16) |
| `ef_construction` | Build-time beam width: better graph, slower build | 64 to 400 (pgvector default 64) |
| `ef_search` | Query-time beam width: tune recall vs latency at runtime | 40 to 400 (pgvector default 40); must be at least k |

- **Memory**: full vectors plus neighbour lists. HNSW is a RAM index; when it does not fit, performance collapses into disk seeks.
- **Build**: inserts are `O(log N)`-ish each but much slower than appends; bulk loads take minutes to hours at tens of millions.
- **Deletes**: usually marked as tombstones; the graph degrades with heavy churn and periodically needs a rebuild or repair.
- **Filtering**: covered below, the most common production problem.

## IVF: cluster, then search a few clusters

An inverted file index runs **k-means** on (a sample of) the vectors to get `nlist` centroids, and assigns each vector to its nearest centroid's list.

```text
build:  k-means -> nlist centroids; each vector goes to the list of its nearest centroid
query:  find the nprobe centroids nearest the query; scan only those lists exactly

nlist = 4,096 lists, N = 10M  -> about 2,400 vectors per list
nprobe = 16                   -> scan about 39,000 vectors instead of 10M (0.4%)
```

The failure mode is the **boundary problem**: the true nearest neighbour sits in a list whose centroid was not among the `nprobe` closest. Raising `nprobe` trades latency for recall, smoothly and at query time. Rules of thumb: Faiss suggests `nlist` somewhere around 4 to 16 times sqrt(N); pgvector's IVFFlat docs suggest `lists = rows / 1000` up to 1M rows and `sqrt(rows)` beyond, with `probes` around sqrt(lists) as a start. IVF builds faster and uses less memory than HNSW, but needs a training step on representative data and degrades if the data distribution drifts after training.

## Product quantisation: compress the vectors themselves

PQ (Jégou, Douze and Schmid, 2011) attacks memory. Split each d-dimensional vector into `m` sub-vectors, run k-means with 256 centroids in each sub-space, and store each sub-vector as the **one-byte id** of its nearest centroid.

```text
d = 768, m = 96 sub-vectors of 8 dims, 256 centroids each (8 bits)
original: 768 x 4 bytes = 3,072 bytes      PQ code: 96 x 1 byte = 96 bytes   (32x smaller)

query time (asymmetric distance computation, ADC):
  1. for each sub-space j, compute the distance from the query's sub-vector to all 256 centroids
     -> a 96 x 256 lookup table, computed once per query
  2. distance(query, x) ~= sum over j of table[j][code_j(x)]   -> 96 table lookups, no multiplies
```

The distances are approximate, so PQ alone loses recall. The standard fix is **rescoring**: take the top few hundred by PQ distance and recompute exact distances with full vectors (kept on disk or in a cheaper tier).

### Combining them

| Index | Memory per 768-d vector | Recall | Build | When |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Flat | 3 KB | 100% | None | Under ~1M, ground truth for measuring others |
| HNSW (float32) | about 3.2 KB | 95 to 99%+ | Slow | Default up to tens of millions, latency-sensitive |
| IVF-Flat | about 3 KB | 90 to 99% (nprobe) | Medium, needs training | Large, cost-sensitive, batch-friendly |
| IVF-PQ | about 100 bytes | Lower; rescoring recovers it | Medium | Hundreds of millions to billions |
| HNSW + scalar/binary quantisation | 0.1 to 0.8 KB | High with rescoring | Slow | Big collections in a vector DB |
| Disk-based graph (DiskANN family) | Compressed in RAM, full on SSD | High | Slow | Larger than RAM |

The Faiss library paper (Douze et al., 2024) is the best single reference for how these compose, and Pinecone's Faiss series has readable walkthroughs of HNSW and PQ.

## Filtered vector search

Real queries come with filters: tenant, permissions, language, date, product. ANN indexes were designed for unfiltered search, and filters break their assumptions.

| Strategy | How | Failure mode |
|---|---|---|
| Post-filter | ANN top-k, then drop rows failing the filter | Selective filters return too few results (top 10, 9 filtered out) |
| Pre-filter (brute force) | Compute the allowed set, exact-search inside it | Fine when the allowed set is small, slow when it is large |
| Filtered graph traversal | Traverse HNSW but only accept matching nodes | When few nodes match, the graph becomes disconnected and recall drops |
| Partition by filter | Separate index per tenant (or per hot filter value) | Many small indexes; great isolation for multi-tenant SaaS |

Good engines pick a strategy based on the estimated filter selectivity (pgvector 0.8 added iterative index scans so a filtered HNSW query keeps scanning until it has enough rows). In an interview, saying "post-filtering drops results under selective filters, so I would use the engine's filtered search, partition per tenant, or over-fetch and verify, and I would test with my most selective filter" signals real experience.

## Measuring an ANN index

Measure ANN recall separately from end-to-end retrieval quality: compute the exact top-k with a flat index for a sample of real queries, then compare the ANN results.

```text
ANN recall@10 = |ANN top-10 intersect exact top-10| / 10
```

Plot recall against p95 latency while sweeping `ef_search` or `nprobe`, pick the knee of the curve, and re-check after large data changes. ANN recall of 0.95 is a good target for RAG; past that, chunking, hybrid search and reranking usually matter far more than the last percent of ANN recall.

# Measure ANN recall against exact search and sweep the recall/latency knob.
# pip install faiss-cpu numpy
import time

import faiss
import numpy as np

d, n, nq, k = 768, 200_000, 500, 10
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
xb = rng.standard_normal((n, d), dtype=np.float32)   # use real embeddings in practice: random data is a worst case
xq = rng.standard_normal((nq, d), dtype=np.float32)
faiss.normalize_L2(xb)
faiss.normalize_L2(xq)

flat = faiss.IndexFlatIP(d)                          # exact inner product == cosine on unit vectors
flat.add(xb)
_, truth = flat.search(xq, k)


def recall(found: np.ndarray) -> float:
    return float(np.mean([len(set(f) & set(t)) / k for f, t in zip(found, truth)]))


def bench(name: str, index: faiss.Index) -> None:
    t = time.perf_counter()
    _, ids = index.search(xq, k)
    ms = (time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000 / nq
    print(f"{name:28s} recall@{k}={recall(ids):.3f}  {ms:.2f} ms/query")


hnsw = faiss.IndexHNSWFlat(d, 32, faiss.METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT)   # M = 32
hnsw.hnsw.efConstruction = 200
hnsw.add(xb)
for ef in (16, 64, 256):
    hnsw.hnsw.efSearch = ef
    bench(f"HNSW M=32 efSearch={ef}", hnsw)

nlist, m = 1024, 96                                   # 96 sub-vectors x 8 bits = 96 bytes per vector
quant = faiss.IndexFlatIP(d)
ivfpq = faiss.IndexIVFPQ(quant, d, nlist, m, 8, faiss.METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT)
ivfpq.train(xb[:100_000])                             # k-means for the lists and the PQ codebooks
ivfpq.add(xb)
for nprobe in (4, 16, 64):
    ivfpq.nprobe = nprobe
    bench(f"IVF-PQ nprobe={nprobe}", ivfpq)

# Rescore: take a PQ shortlist, recompute exact scores with full vectors.
ivfpq.nprobe = 16
_, short = ivfpq.search(xq, 100)
rescored = np.stack([s[np.argsort(-(xb[s] @ q))][:k] for s, q in zip(short, xq)])
print(f"{'IVF-PQ + exact rescoring':28s} recall@{k}={recall(rescored):.3f}")

parts.body:
## Lexical retrieval: BM25 under the hood

BM25 is the ranking function behind Lucene, Elasticsearch, OpenSearch and most "keyword search". It scores a document D for a query Q as a sum over query terms:

```text
score(D, Q) = sum over terms t in Q of
              IDF(t) * f(t, D) * (k1 + 1) / ( f(t, D) + k1 * (1 - b + b * |D| / avgdl) )

f(t, D)  = how often t appears in D           IDF(t) = log(1 + (N - n_t + 0.5) / (n_t + 0.5))
|D|      = document length, avgdl = average   k1 ~ 1.2 (term-frequency saturation), b ~ 0.75 (length normalisation)
```

What each piece buys you:

- **IDF**: rare terms ("XR-2041-B", "Kubernetes") count far more than common ones ("the", "how").
- **Saturation (k1)**: the tenth occurrence of a term adds much less than the first, so keyword stuffing does not win.
- **Length normalisation (b)**: a match in a short chunk counts more than the same match in a long one.

BM25 is fast (inverted index, only documents containing a query term are scored), needs no training, and is excellent at exact tokens. Its weaknesses are vocabulary mismatch (no synonyms or paraphrase) and dependence on tokenisation: an analyser that splits `XR-2041-B` into `xr`, `2041`, `b` loses much of the benefit. Configure analysers for identifiers, and consider a separate keyword field for codes.

**Learned sparse retrieval** (SPLADE and similar) sits between the two worlds: a transformer predicts weighted terms for each document, including expansion terms that do not appear in the text, and the result is stored in an ordinary inverted index. It recovers some paraphrase handling while keeping exact-match strength, at the cost of model inference at indexing time.

## Fusing dense and sparse results

You now have two ranked lists with incompatible scores: cosine similarities squeezed into a narrow band, and unbounded BM25 scores whose scale depends on the query. Three ways to combine them:

| Method | How | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reciprocal rank fusion | `sum 1 / (k + rank)` per list, k = 60 | No tuning, robust to score scales | Ignores how confident each retriever was |
| Convex combination | Normalise each score (min-max or z-score per query), then `alpha * dense + (1 - alpha) * sparse` | Uses score magnitudes; alpha can be tuned | Normalisation is fragile; alpha needs a labelled set |
| Learned fusion | A small model or the reranker decides | Best quality | Needs training data |

### RRF in more detail

RRF comes from Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher (SIGIR 2009). The constant k damps the influence of top ranks: with k = 60, rank 1 contributes 1/61 = 0.0164 and rank 10 contributes 1/70 = 0.0143, so a document that appears in **both** lists at moderate ranks beats a document that is first in only one list. That is exactly the behaviour you want when the two retrievers fail in different ways.

Practical details:

- Fuse the top 20 to 100 from each retriever, not the top 5; fusion cannot rescue what was cut.
- Weighted RRF (`w_i / (k + rank_i)`) lets you lean on one retriever for a query class (for example, boost BM25 when the query contains an identifier).
- Deduplicate by chunk id before fusing, and dedupe near-identical chunks after.
- Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Weaviate, Qdrant, MongoDB Atlas and others offer built-in hybrid queries with RRF; in Postgres you can do it in one SQL statement (see the code).

## Reranking: why cross-encoders are more accurate

The embedding model in stage 1 is a **bi-encoder**: it encodes the query and each document **separately** into vectors and compares them with a dot product. That separation is what makes it fast (documents are encoded once, offline) and what limits it: the document vector was computed without knowing the question, so it has to summarise everything the document might be asked about into one point.

A **cross-encoder** reads the query and the document **together** in one transformer pass (`[CLS] query [SEP] passage [SEP]`) and outputs a single relevance score. Every query token can attend to every passage token, so it can check that the passage answers *this* question: that "refund" relates to "EU customers" and not to "US customers", that a negation is present, that the number matches. Nogueira and Cho's monoBERT (2019) showed the size of this jump on MS MARCO, and every serious retrieval stack since has used the pattern.

```text
bi-encoder:     q -> enc -> vq       d -> enc -> vd (offline)     score = vq . vd
cross-encoder:  [q ; d] -> enc -> score                            (one pass per pair, online)
late interaction (ColBERT):  q -> token vectors Q;  d -> token vectors D (offline)
                score = sum over q-tokens of max over d-tokens of (Qi . Dj)   "MaxSim"
```

**ColBERT** (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020) is the middle ground: keep one vector per token for every document (precomputed), and score with MaxSim. Nearly cross-encoder quality, precomputable, but storage multiplies by the number of tokens per chunk (mitigated by compression in later versions).

### Cost and latency

A cross-encoder runs one forward pass per (query, candidate) pair, and nothing is precomputable. Reranking 50 candidates of about 300 tokens means 50 sequences of roughly 330 tokens: small rerankers on a GPU do this in tens of milliseconds, large ones or CPU inference in hundreds. That is why you rerank 20 to 100 candidates, not 10,000. Options:

| Reranker type | Examples | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Hosted rerank APIs | Cohere Rerank, Voyage, Jina | One HTTP call with the query and candidate list; per-search pricing |
| Open cross-encoders | `ms-marco-MiniLM` family, BGE rerankers | Self-host on CPU or GPU; small ones are cheap |
| LLM as reranker | Pointwise ("score 0-3"), listwise ("order these 20 passages") | Most flexible, can use instructions, slowest and most expensive; watch position bias |

### What reranking fixes and what it does not

Reranking fixes **ordering**: the right passage was in the top 50 but at rank 23. It cannot fix **recall**: if the passage is not in the candidate set, no reranker can find it. So the diagnosis order is always: measure recall@50 of stage 1 first; if it is low, fix chunking, hybrid search or query rewriting; only then tune the reranker on precision metrics like nDCG@5 or MRR.

Rerankers also give you a **calibrated-ish relevance score** that is much better than cosine for deciding "nothing relevant was found, say so" (still tune the threshold on labelled data).

## Retrieval metrics you should be able to define

| Metric | Definition | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| Recall@k | Share of queries (or relevant docs) found in the top k | Stage 1 and fusion: did we get it at all? |
| Precision@k | Share of the top k that is relevant | What reaches the prompt |
| MRR | Mean of 1 / rank of the first relevant result | Single-answer lookup |
| nDCG@k | Graded relevance, discounted by log2(rank + 1), normalised to the ideal ordering | Reranker quality with graded labels |
| Hit rate | At least one relevant result in top k | Simple dashboards |

Report them per **slice** (identifier queries, multi-hop questions, recent documents, each tenant) because averages hide exactly the failures users complain about.

# Self-hosted second stage: weighted RRF over several retrievers, then a cross-encoder, with nDCG@k to compare.
# pip install sentence-transformers numpy
import math
from collections import defaultdict

from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder

reranker = CrossEncoder("cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2", max_length=512)


def rrf(ranked_lists: dict[str, list[str]], weights: dict[str, float] | None = None, k: int = 60) -> list[str]:
    scores: dict[str, float] = defaultdict(float)
    for name, ids in ranked_lists.items():
        w = (weights or {}).get(name, 1.0)
        for rank, doc_id in enumerate(dict.fromkeys(ids), start=1):   # dedupe, keep first rank
            scores[doc_id] += w / (k + rank)
    return sorted(scores, key=scores.get, reverse=True)


def rerank(query: str, ids: list[str], text: dict[str, str], top_n: int = 5) -> list[tuple[str, float]]:
    pairs = [(query, text[i]) for i in ids]
    scores = reranker.predict(pairs, batch_size=32)                  # one forward pass per pair
    return sorted(zip(ids, map(float, scores)), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)[:top_n]


def ndcg_at_k(ranked: list[str], gains: dict[str, int], k: int = 5) -> float:
    dcg = sum(gains.get(d, 0) / math.log2(i + 2) for i, d in enumerate(ranked[:k]))
    ideal = sorted(gains.values(), reverse=True)[:k]
    idcg = sum(g / math.log2(i + 2) for i, g in enumerate(ideal))
    return dcg / idcg if idcg else 0.0


def search(query: str, dense: list[str], bm25: list[str], text: dict[str, str]) -> list[tuple[str, float]]:
    has_identifier = any(ch.isdigit() for ch in query) and "-" in query
    weights = {"bm25": 1.5, "dense": 1.0} if has_identifier else None   # lean on lexical for codes
    fused = rrf({"dense": dense[:50], "bm25": bm25[:50]}, weights)
    return rerank(query, fused[:50], text)

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are testing

Retrieval questions probe whether you understand the machinery, not just the vocabulary. Strong candidates explain HNSW and IVF in a few sentences each, know which knob trades recall for latency, can do memory arithmetic, explain *why* a cross-encoder beats a bi-encoder, and diagnose in the right order: recall first, then ranking. They also know filtered search is where vector databases hurt in production.

## Questions with model answers

### 1. Explain HNSW to me as if I were a backend engineer who knows skip lists.

**Model answer.** It is a skip list made of graphs. Every vector is a node on layer 0 with links to its nearest neighbours; a random, exponentially shrinking subset also appears on higher layers with longer-range links. To search, you start at the entry point on the top layer and greedily hop to whichever neighbour is closest to the query until you cannot improve, then drop a layer and repeat. On layer 0 you run a beam search keeping the best `ef_search` candidates and return the top k. `M` controls links per node (recall and memory), `ef_construction` controls graph quality at build time, and `ef_search` is the runtime recall versus latency dial. Costs: it lives in RAM, inserts are slow compared with appends, and deletes are tombstones that degrade the graph until a rebuild.

### 2. HNSW or IVF-PQ for 500 million 768-dimensional vectors?

**Model answer.** Do the arithmetic first: 500M x 768 x 4 bytes is about 1.5 TB of float32 vectors, so plain HNSW means a large sharded RAM cluster. IVF-PQ with 96-byte codes is about 48 GB plus centroids, which fits on a few machines. I would use IVF-PQ (or a disk-based graph index with compressed vectors in RAM) as the first stage, over-fetch a few hundred candidates, rescore them with full-precision vectors from SSD, then rerank. I would tune `nlist`, `nprobe` and the rescoring depth by plotting recall@k against p95 latency on real queries, using exact search on a sample as ground truth.

### 3. Why does hybrid search help, and why RRF instead of adding the scores?

**Model answer.** Dense and lexical retrieval fail differently: embeddings handle paraphrase but blur exact identifiers and rare names; BM25 nails exact tokens but misses synonyms. Fusing them recovers both kinds of query. Adding raw scores is fragile because cosine values sit in a narrow band and BM25 scores are unbounded and query-dependent. RRF uses only ranks, `1 / (60 + rank)` summed across lists, so it needs no normalisation or tuning, and documents that appear in both lists rise to the top. If I have labelled data, I might tune a weighted RRF or a normalised convex combination, but RRF is the robust default.

### 4. Why is a cross-encoder more accurate than the embedding model, and why not use it for the first stage?

**Model answer.** A bi-encoder compresses each document into a vector without seeing the query, then compares vectors. A cross-encoder reads the query and passage together, so attention can check how they relate: the right entity, the negation, the matching number. That is much more accurate. But it needs one forward pass per pair at query time and nothing can be precomputed, so scoring millions of documents is impossible. The pattern is a cheap high-recall first stage to get 50 to 100 candidates, then a cross-encoder to pick the best 3 to 10. ColBERT-style late interaction is a middle ground with precomputed token vectors.

### 5. Our tenants complain that search returns nothing even though the documents exist. We use a vector DB with a tenant filter. What is going on?

**Model answer.** Almost certainly post-filtering: the ANN index returns the global top-k, then the tenant filter removes most of them, so small tenants get few or zero results. Fixes depend on the engine: use native filtered search that applies the filter during traversal, enable iterative scanning (for example pgvector's iterative index scans), over-fetch heavily, or partition the index per tenant, which also gives cleaner isolation. Very selective filters can also disconnect the HNSW graph during filtered traversal, so for tiny tenants exact search over their own rows is often best. I would add per-tenant recall checks to the eval.

### 6. Retrieval quality is poor. How do you decide between improving the retriever and adding a reranker?

**Model answer.** Measure recall@50 of the first stage against a labelled set. If the gold passage is usually not in the top 50, a reranker cannot help; I need to fix chunking, add hybrid search, add query rewriting, or switch embedding models. If recall@50 is high but recall@5 or nDCG@5 is low, the right passage is retrieved but ranked badly, which is exactly what a reranker fixes. I check these per slice, such as identifier queries or multi-hop questions, because averages hide the failing class.

### 7. How would you set a "no relevant results" threshold?

**Model answer.** Not on raw cosine: those scores are model-specific and compressed. A reranker's score is a better signal. I would label a few hundred query-passage pairs as relevant or not, look at the score distributions, and pick a threshold that hits the precision I want for the "I could not find this" behaviour, then monitor how often it fires in production. I would re-calibrate whenever the reranker or embedding model changes.

### 8. Define recall@k, MRR and nDCG and say when you would use each.

**Model answer.** Recall@k is the share of relevant items that appear in the top k; I use it for candidate generation because the only question there is "did we get it at all". MRR is the mean of 1 over the rank of the first relevant result; good when there is a single correct passage. nDCG@k uses graded relevance and discounts lower positions logarithmically, normalised by the best possible ordering; I use it to compare rerankers when several passages are partially relevant.

## Common mistakes

- Tuning the reranker when the real problem is first-stage recall.
- Fusing only the top 5 from each retriever, which leaves fusion nothing to work with.
- Post-filtering after ANN with selective filters, then blaming the embedding model.
- Using an analyser that shreds identifiers, so BM25 cannot match them.
- Reporting ANN recall as if it were end-to-end retrieval quality, or vice versa.
- Reranking hundreds or thousands of candidates per request and then blaming the latency.
- Forgetting that HNSW deletes are tombstones and that heavy churn degrades the graph.

## Numbers to have ready

| Item | Typical value |
|---|---|
| RRF constant k | 60 |
| BM25 k1 / b | 1.2 / 0.75 |
| HNSW M / ef_construction / ef_search (pgvector defaults) | 16 / 64 / 40 |
| PQ code size, 768-d, m = 96 | 96 bytes (32x smaller than float32) |
| Candidates into the reranker | 20 to 100 |
| Passages into the prompt | 3 to 10 |

keyPoints: Retrieval is a funnel: cheap high-recall candidate generation, rank fusion, then an expensive high-precision reranker on a few dozen candidates.
HNSW is a layered proximity graph; M and ef_construction set quality and memory, ef_search is the runtime recall-latency dial.
IVF searches only nprobe k-means clusters; PQ compresses vectors to m one-byte codes with table-lookup distances; rescore shortlists with full vectors.
Post-filtering after ANN starves selective filters; use filtered traversal, iterative scans, per-tenant partitions or exact search for small sets.
BM25 wins on exact tokens, dense on paraphrase; RRF fuses ranks without score normalisation and rewards agreement.
Cross-encoders read query and passage together and beat bi-encoders on precision but cannot be precomputed; ColBERT sits in between.
Diagnose recall@50 before tuning the reranker; report recall, MRR and nDCG per query slice.

check.q: In a pgvector HNSW index, recall is slightly too low but build time and memory are acceptable. Which change is cheapest to try first?
options: Rebuild the index with a larger M
Raise ef_search for queries
Switch to IVFFlat
Increase the embedding dimensions
check.why: ef_search is a query-time setting: no rebuild needed, and it directly trades latency for recall. M and ef_construction require rebuilding.

They tie
The document found by both, because 1/63 + 1/64 is larger than 1/61
It depends on the raw cosine scores
check.why: 1/63 + 1/64 is about 0.0315 versus 1/61 at about 0.0164. RRF rewards agreement between retrievers and ignores raw scores.

options: Raise recall@50 to above 0.9
Improve ordering within the candidates but cannot recover the 38% of queries whose gold passage was never retrieved
Nothing, because rerankers only work with BM25
Reduce latency
check.why: A reranker only reorders the candidates it receives. Low first-stage recall must be fixed with chunking, hybrid search, query rewriting or a better embedding model.

parts.label: Query side
parts.body:
## When basic RAG stops being enough

A well-built basic pipeline (structural chunks, hybrid search, reranker, grounded prompt) answers most single-hop factual questions. It breaks on four kinds of input, and each "advanced RAG" technique targets one of them:

| Failure | Example | Technique family |
|---|---|---|
| The query does not look like the answer | "my card got declined abroad" vs a doc titled "International transaction limits" | Query rewriting, HyDE, multi-query |
| The question needs several pieces of evidence | "Which of our EU suppliers had incidents after the 2024 audit?" | Decomposition, iterative and agentic retrieval |
| The question is about the whole corpus | "What are the main complaints across all Q3 tickets?" | GraphRAG and hierarchical summaries |
| The evidence is not text | A chart in a PDF, a scanned form, an architecture diagram | Multimodal retrieval |

The rule of thumb: **add a technique only when your eval shows the failure it fixes**. Each one adds latency, cost and new ways to fail. This part covers the query side; the next covers structure (graphs, agents, multimodal); then evaluation, which decides whether any of it helped.

## Query rewriting

Users write queries for humans, not retrievers. A rewriting step uses a small, fast LLM to turn the raw input into one or more retrieval-friendly queries.

### Conversational condensation

In chat, follow-ups depend on history: "and for Germany?" retrieves nothing useful on its own. Condense the last few turns plus the follow-up into a **standalone question** ("What is the refund window for customers in Germany?") and retrieve with that. This is the single highest-value rewrite for any chat product, and it is cheap.

### Expansion and normalisation

- Expand acronyms and internal jargon using a glossary in the prompt ("PTO" to "paid time off").
- Fix typos and normalise product names.
- Extract **filters** into structured fields (`{"country": "DE", "doc_type": "policy", "after": "2025-01-01"}`), which then become metadata filters instead of noisy query words. This is often called self-querying.

### Multi-query and RAG-Fusion

Generate 3 to 5 paraphrases or sub-angles of the question, retrieve for each, and fuse the lists with RRF. It improves recall when users phrase things unpredictably, at the cost of N retrievals (run in parallel) and one LLM call. Watch for **query drift**: paraphrases that wander away from the user's intent drag in off-topic chunks, so keep the original query in the set and give it extra weight.

### Decomposition and step-back

- **Decomposition**: split a compound question into sub-questions ("Which suppliers are in the EU?", "Which suppliers had incidents after March 2024?"), retrieve for each, and answer from the combined evidence. Static decomposition works when sub-questions are independent; when one depends on the answer of another, you need iterative retrieval (next part).
- **Step-back prompting** (Zheng et al., 2023): ask a more general question first ("What are the rules for data retention under GDPR?") to retrieve principles, alongside the specific one.

## HyDE: search with a fake answer

Hypothetical Document Embeddings (Gao et al., 2022) start from an observation: questions and answers live in different regions of embedding space, but **two answers** to the same question are close to each other. So:

1. Ask an LLM to write a plausible answer passage for the question, without retrieval. It may contain wrong facts; that does not matter.
2. Embed the **hypothetical passage** (optionally averaged with the query embedding).
3. Search with that vector. Real passages that "look like the answer" come back.
4. Generate the final answer from the real passages, never from the hypothetical one.

```text
query:        "can I get my money back if I cancel after two weeks in Spain?"
hypothetical: "Customers in the EU may request a refund within 14 days of purchase.
               After this period, refunds are at the discretion of support..."
-> the hypothetical's embedding lands near the actual refund policy chunk
```

When it helps: short or vague queries, zero-shot domains with no labelled data, and asymmetric models that were not trained on question-passage pairs. When it hurts: queries about entities the LLM knows nothing about (the hypothetical invents the wrong vocabulary), exact-identifier queries (BM25 already wins), and latency-sensitive paths (an extra generation of 100 to 200 tokens before retrieval can start). It also leaks the query to whichever model writes the hypothetical, which matters for regulated data.

## Query routing

Not every query should hit the same index, or any index at all.

```text
"hi, thanks!"                      -> no retrieval, short reply
"what's our parental leave policy" -> HR policy index
"error E-4012 when syncing"        -> support KB + ticket history, BM25-weighted
"how many tickets mentioned SSO"   -> SQL over the ticket table, not RAG
"summarise themes across Q3"       -> global/summary index (GraphRAG-style)
```

A router can be a small classifier, embedding similarity to labelled example queries, or an LLM call with structured output (enum of routes plus extracted filters). Routing is a **workflow**, not an agent: the routes are known in advance. Measure router accuracy on its own eval slice because a wrong route makes every downstream metric look bad.

## Where query transformations go wrong

- **Latency stacking**: condense (300 ms) plus multi-query (500 ms) plus HyDE (700 ms) before retrieval even starts. Run independent steps in parallel, use the smallest model that passes the eval, and skip transformations for queries that are already clear (a cheap classifier can decide).
- **Hallucinated constraints**: the rewriter adds a filter the user never asked for ("after 2024"). Validate extracted filters against allowed values and log original and rewritten queries side by side.
- **Over-rewriting identifiers**: an LLM "corrects" `XR-2041-B` into something else. Copy identifiers through verbatim, or retrieve with both the original and the rewrite.
- **Evaluation blind spots**: if you only evaluate end-to-end answers, you cannot tell whether a regression came from the rewriter. Log and score each stage.

parts.label: Graphs and agents
parts.body:
## GraphRAG: answering questions about the whole corpus

Vector retrieval finds **passages similar to the query**. Some questions have no such passage: "What are the main themes in these 5,000 customer interviews?" or "How are our vendors connected to the 2025 outages?" The answer is spread thinly across the corpus, so top-k retrieval returns ten random fragments and the model summarises those.

Microsoft's GraphRAG paper (Edge et al., 2024, "From Local to Global") builds structure at indexing time:

1. **Extract**: an LLM reads every chunk and extracts entities (people, organisations, systems, concepts), relationships between them, and short claims, with descriptions.
2. **Build a graph**: merge duplicate entities across chunks; edges carry relationship descriptions and weights.
3. **Detect communities**: run hierarchical community detection (Leiden) to group densely connected entities, at several levels of granularity.
4. **Summarise communities**: an LLM writes a report for each community at each level, bottom-up.

At query time there are two main modes:

- **Global search** (sensemaking questions): map-reduce over community reports. Each report produces a partial answer with a helpfulness score (map), then the best partial answers are combined into the final answer (reduce). This is what plain RAG cannot do.
- **Local search** (entity-centred questions): find entities matching the query, then gather their neighbours, relationships, claims, community reports and the source chunks into the context.

### Costs and when it is worth it

| Aspect | Plain vector RAG | GraphRAG |
|---|---|---|
| Indexing cost | Embedding calls only | Several LLM calls per chunk plus community summaries: often 10 to 100x more expensive |
| Updates | Re-embed changed chunks | Re-extract, re-merge, and potentially re-summarise affected communities |
| Global "themes" questions | Weak | Strong |
| Multi-hop entity questions | Moderate (with iterative retrieval) | Strong when the extraction is good |
| Single-hop factual lookup | Strong, cheap | No better, more expensive |
| Failure mode | Missed passages | Bad entity resolution ("AWS" vs "Amazon Web Services"), hallucinated edges |

Microsoft later published variants that move most of the LLM work from indexing to query time (LazyGraphRAG) because full indexing is costly. The interview-worthy point: **GraphRAG is a precomputed summary hierarchy plus an entity graph; use it when your eval has sensemaking or relationship-heavy questions, not as a default**. A simpler alternative for "summarise everything" questions is a hierarchical summary tree (summaries of clusters of chunks, as in RAPTOR) or just a batch map-reduce job.

## Agentic RAG: retrieval as a tool in a loop

Basic RAG retrieves once, before generation. **Agentic RAG** gives the model a search tool and lets it decide when to search, with what query, and whether the results are good enough, inside an agent loop (see the agents chapter).

```text
question -> model: "I need X"  -> search("X")      -> results
         -> model: "X mentions supplier list; now need incidents after 2024-03"
                                -> search("incidents supplier A after March 2024") -> results
         -> model: "enough evidence" -> answer with citations
```

It shines on multi-hop questions, ambiguous questions where the first search reveals the right vocabulary, and research-style tasks across several sources (docs, SQL, web). It costs more: several model calls and searches per question (typically 2 to 10x the tokens of single-shot RAG), higher and more variable latency, and new failure modes (looping on the same query, stopping too early, wandering off topic). Anthropic's write-up of its multi-agent research system describes the same pattern scaled up, with parallel subagents each running their own search loops.

Two research ideas worth knowing by name, because interviewers like them:

- **Self-RAG** (Asai et al., 2023) trains a model to emit special reflection tokens that decide whether to retrieve, judge whether each passage is relevant, and check whether the generated text is supported. Production systems rarely fine-tune for this, but they copy the idea with prompted checks.
- **Corrective RAG (CRAG)** (Yan et al., 2024) adds a lightweight retrieval evaluator that grades retrieved documents as correct, incorrect or ambiguous; incorrect triggers a fallback such as web search, and documents are refined to their relevant strips before generation.

The practical pattern that falls out of both is **retrieve, grade, then act**: grade the retrieved passages (a reranker threshold or a small LLM judge), and if they are insufficient, rewrite the query and retry, widen the search, switch source, or abstain. Bound it: at most 2 to 3 retrieval rounds, a token budget, and a clear abstain path.

## Long context vs retrieval, and context assembly

Models now accept hundreds of thousands to millions of tokens, but research such as "Lost in the Middle" (Liu et al., 2023) showed that models use information at the start and end of a long context more reliably than in the middle, and every token costs money and latency on every request. Practical consequences for assembly:

- Put the highest-ranked passages first (or first and last), not in arbitrary order.
- Prefer 5 well-chosen passages over 40 loosely related ones; extra irrelevant context measurably hurts faithfulness.
- For a handful of long documents used in one session, loading them whole with prompt caching can beat chunking; for a large or permissioned corpus, retrieval still wins.
- **Context compression**: extract only the relevant sentences from each passage (with a small model or a reranker at sentence level) before generation.

## Multimodal RAG

Enterprise knowledge lives in PDFs with charts, tables, scanned forms, slides and diagrams. Three architectures:

| Approach | How | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| Convert to text | OCR plus layout parsing; tables to markdown; a vision model captions figures | Reuses the text pipeline and BM25 | Captions lose detail; parsing errors are silent |
| Multimodal embeddings | Embed images and text into one space (CLIP-style models) | Text-to-image search | Weak on dense document pages |
| Page-image retrieval | Embed each page **as an image** with a vision-language model, multi-vector late interaction (ColPali) | No OCR pipeline; keeps layout, charts and tables | Many vectors per page (storage); needs a vision model for generation too |

ColPali (Faysse et al., 2024) embeds page screenshots into patch-level vectors and scores them against query token vectors with ColBERT-style MaxSim; on the paper's visually rich document benchmark it beat OCR-based text pipelines while removing most of the parsing work. Whichever retrieval you choose, generation needs a vision-capable model if you pass page images, and citations should point to the page number and ideally the region.

## Putting it together: a maturity ladder

```text
1. basic:      structural chunks + dense search + grounded prompt with citations
2. solid:      + hybrid BM25 + reranker + conversational rewrite + ACL filters
3. targeted:   + HyDE / multi-query / routing  (only for slices where the eval shows misses)
4. iterative:  + retrieve-grade-retry loop or agentic search for multi-hop questions
5. structural: + GraphRAG / summary trees for corpus-level questions; multimodal for visual docs
```

Most products should live at level 2 and add level 3 to 5 techniques per failure slice. That sentence, backed by an eval, is a strong senior answer.

parts.label: Evaluation
parts.body:
## Why RAG evaluation needs its own vocabulary

A RAG answer can be wrong for at least five different reasons: the document was never ingested, retrieval missed it, ranking buried it, the model ignored it, or the model added things that were not in it. A single "answer quality" score cannot tell these apart, and every advanced technique in this lesson targets a different one. So RAG evaluation scores **components** and **end-to-end** separately.

```text
             retrieval metrics                 generation metrics
question -> [retriever] -> contexts -> [generator] -> answer
              |                          |
   context recall / precision      faithfulness (answer vs contexts)
   recall@k, MRR, nDCG             answer relevance (answer vs question)
                                   correctness (answer vs reference)
```

## The core metrics

The RAGAS paper (Es et al., 2023) popularised reference-free metrics computed with an LLM; the names are now standard across tools.

| Metric | Question it answers | How it is computed | Needs a reference? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Context recall | Did retrieval bring back everything needed? | Split the reference answer into claims; check each claim is supported by the retrieved contexts | Yes (reference answer or gold passages) |
| Context precision | Is what we retrieved relevant, and ranked high? | Judge each retrieved chunk relevant or not; weight by rank | Optional |
| Faithfulness (groundedness) | Is every claim in the answer supported by the contexts? | Extract claims from the answer; verify each against the contexts; supported / total | No |
| Answer relevance | Does the answer address the question? | Judge directly, or generate questions from the answer and compare with the original | No |
| Answer correctness | Is it actually right? | Compare with a reference answer (claim overlap or a judge) | Yes |
| Citation accuracy | Do the cited sources support the sentences they are attached to? | Per-citation entailment check | No |

Two subtle points interviewers like:

- **Faithful is not the same as correct.** If retrieval returned an outdated policy, a perfectly faithful answer is still wrong. That is why you need both groundedness and correctness, and why ingestion freshness is part of quality.
- **Abstention is a feature.** Include questions whose answer is not in the corpus (or is in a document the test user cannot access). The correct output is "I could not find this". Score abstention precision and recall separately; a system that never abstains will hallucinate, and one that always abstains is useless.

## Building the eval set

1. **Seed with real questions**: from search logs, support tickets, Slack, or a pilot. Real phrasing matters more than volume.
2. **Synthetic generation to fill gaps**: have an LLM read sampled chunks and write questions answerable from them, recording the source chunk as gold. Then filter: remove questions that copy the chunk's wording verbatim (they make dense retrieval look better than it is), questions answerable without the document, and ambiguous ones. Have a human review a sample.
3. **Tag slices**: single-hop, multi-hop, identifier lookup, comparison, temporal ("latest", "after 2024"), corpus-level, unanswerable, permission-restricted, each language.
4. **Label gold evidence**: the chunk ids (or document plus section) that answer each question, so you can compute retrieval metrics without an LLM. Chunk ids change when you re-chunk, so label at document or section level and map.
5. **Grow from failures**: every production bug and every thumbs-down that reveals a real failure becomes a case.

A useful size: 100 to 300 cases to start, enough for differences of a few points to be distinguishable from noise on the slices you care about.

## LLM judges for RAG, done carefully

Faithfulness and relevance need a judge model. The general LLM-as-judge rules (covered in the production chapter) apply, plus RAG specifics:

- Judge **claim by claim** rather than "is this answer faithful, 1 to 10". Claim-level binary decisions are more reliable and give you a ratio.
- Give the judge exactly the contexts the generator saw, in the same order.
- Calibrate against 50 to 100 human-labelled examples; report agreement (accuracy, or Cohen's kappa) before trusting the judge in CI.
- Use a different model family or at least a different prompt from the generator to reduce self-preference bias.
- Cache judge outputs keyed by (question, contexts, answer, judge prompt version); evals become cheap to re-run.

## Evaluating the advanced techniques

Every technique should be justified by a slice metric moving:

| Technique | Metric that should improve | Metric to watch for regressions |
|---|---|---|
| Contextual chunks, late chunking | Context recall on ambiguous-reference questions | Ingestion cost, index size |
| Hybrid + RRF | Recall@20 on identifier slice | Latency |
| Reranker | nDCG@5, context precision | p95 latency |
| Query rewriting / HyDE | Recall on vague and conversational slices | Recall on identifier slice (drift), latency |
| Agentic / corrective loops | Correctness on multi-hop slice | Cost per query, p95 latency, loop rate |
| GraphRAG | Judge-rated comprehensiveness on corpus-level slice | Indexing cost, freshness lag |

## Online evaluation

Offline evals cannot cover everything users ask. In production:

- Log for every request: original and rewritten query, retrieved ids and scores, reranked ids, prompt version, answer, citations, latency per stage, cost.
- Run a cheap faithfulness check on a sample of traffic (for example 5%), and alert on drift.
- Collect explicit feedback (thumbs, "this source was wrong") and implicit signals (copying the answer, clicking citations, rephrasing immediately, escalating to a human).
- Review a sample of low-scoring traces every week and turn real failures into eval cases. Hamel Husain's writing on error analysis makes the point bluntly: looking at your data beats adding metrics.

## A minimal regression gate

On every change to chunking, embedding model, retrieval settings, prompts or models: run the eval set, compare with the last accepted baseline per slice, and block the merge if recall@k, faithfulness or correctness drop beyond a noise threshold on any critical slice, or if any must-pass case (permissions, unanswerable) fails. The code in this part shows the skeleton.
